paraphrase: Chapter 3 (Vibhūti-pāda, 55 sūtras; the bhāṣya's colophon names it 'vibhūti-pāda'). (1) 3.1-3.8: the last three limbs, concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna) and samādhi, and saṃyama as the three on one object; mastery gives the light of insight; application by stages; the three are inner relative to the earlier limbs and outer relative to the seedless samādhi. (2) 3.9-3.15: the transformations of the mind (of restraint, of samādhi, of one-pointedness) and the transformations of property, characteristic and condition in elements and senses; the property-bearer; sequence as the cause of difference of transformation. (3) 3.16-3.49: what the text says follows from saṃyama on various objects, in groups: past and future, the cries of beings, former births, another's mind, disappearance, the end of life, strengths, the subtle and distant, the worlds, the stars, the body (3.16-3.29); places in the body, prātibha, the heart, knowledge of puruṣa, the arisings of 3.36 (3.30-3.36); the statement that these are obstacles in samādhi and powers for the outgoing mind (3.37); entering another body, mastery of udāna and samāna, divine hearing, going in the sky, the Great Bodiless, mastery of elements, the eight lordly powers, perfection of the body, mastery of the senses, the three madhu-pratīkā powers (3.38-3.48); overlordship of all states and omniscience (3.49). (4) 3.50: from dispassion even towards that, with the seeds of defect destroyed, kaivalya. (5) 3.51: the warning about attachment and pride when invited by those of high stations. (6) 3.52-3.55: saṃyama on the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discrimination, discernment of like things, the saving knowledge, and kaivalya when sattva and puruṣa are equal in purity. The chapter thus sets the powers between the practice of saṃyama and kaivalya, and itself states that they are obstacles for a mind in samādhi (3.37) and are to be met with dispassion (3.50) and without attachment or pride (3.51).

paraphrase: A property is the capacity (śakti) of the property-bearer as delimited by its fitness (yogyatā), inferred from the differences in what it brings forth. The bearer is distinguished from its calmed and undesignable properties while it is experiencing its own function in the present; when it is joined with them only in general form, nothing distinguishes it. The calmed properties are those that have acted and ceased; the arisen are active; the undesignable are those in the state 'everything is of the nature of everything' (sarvaṃ sarvātmakam). The bhāṣya argues that the bearer abides through manifest and unmanifest properties, and that for one for whom this is only properties without a continuing bearer (niranvaya) there would be no enjoyment (bhoga), since an act done by one cognition could not be enjoyed by another; there would be no memory, since what one has seen another cannot remember; and recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of a thing shows that the abiding bearer stands.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: The bhāṣya argues against an unnamed view that there are only properties with no abiding bearer; it names no school. Recorded here as a positioned argument, not as a report of a named opponent.

paraphrase: Where a single bearer would seem to have a single transformation, difference of sequence is the cause of difference of transformations. Sequence is defined as: the property immediately next after a property is its sequence (e.g. powder, lump, pot, shard, grain of clay). Illustrated for the property-transformation (lump ceases, pot arises), the characteristic-transformation (pot from future to present, lump from present to past; the past has no sequence since there is no 'before and after' in it) and the condition-transformation (a new pot's oldness, shown by a succession of moments); the last is a third transformation, distinct from those of property and characteristic. paraphrase: The bhāṣya holds that speech has meaning in its sounds (varṇa); the ear has only the modification of sound as its object; a word (pada) is grasped by the intellect that gathers up the sounds in order. The convention (saṃketa) linking word and meaning is a mutual superimposition, remembered as 'this word is this object, this object is this word'. So word, object and cognition ('cow' as sound, as thing, as cognition) are confused through mutual superimposition. Whoever knows their distinction knows everything (sarvavit). The bhāṣya gives examples showing that the word, the object and the cognition do not go together ('the palace whitens' as action, 'the white palace' as factor), the white object being the support of both word and cognition.

paraphrase: The bhāṣya lays out five forms of the elements. The first, the gross, is the particular things such as sound with shape and other properties. paraphrase: Thus addressed, he should reflect on the faults of attachment: cooked in the terrible coals of saṃsāra and turning in the darkness of birth and death, he has somehow obtained the lamp of yoga that destroys the darkness of the afflictions, and these winds of sense-objects, born of craving, are its opponents; having obtained the light, how should he, deceived by this mirage of sense-objects, make himself fuel again for the blazing fire of saṃsāra? 'Farewell, sense-objects, like dreams, sought by wretched people.' With his mind thus settled he should cultivate samādhi. Having made no attachment, he should not even feel pride ('even the gods seek me'): through pride he would think himself well established and would not regard himself as seized by death by the hair. And heedlessness (pramāda), watching for a gap and to be guarded against with constant effort, having found an opening would stir up the afflictions, and then again there is the prospect of the undesirable. For one who makes neither attachment nor pride, the cultivated aim will be firm and the aim to be cultivated will come to face him.

paraphrase: There is no aggregation of things in the moment and its sequence; muhūrta, day and night and the like are aggregations made by the intellect (buddhi-samāhāra). This time, though empty of a real thing (vastu-śūnya), is a construction of the intellect, following word-cognition, and appears to ordinary people with outgoing vision as if it were the own-form of a thing. The moment rests on things and depends on sequence; sequence is the immediacy of a moment after the earlier one; two moments do not exist together, so only the one present moment exists and no earlier or later moments, and hence there is no aggregate of moments. Past and future moments are to be explained as accompanied by transformation; by that one moment the whole world undergoes transformation, and all these properties rest on that moment. From saṃyama on the moment and its sequence comes direct realisation of them, and from that knowledge born of discrimination arises.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: When the intellect-sattva, with the stain of rajas and tamas shaken off, has as its only remaining scope the cognition of the distinctness of puruṣa and its seeds of affliction are burnt, it comes as if to a likeness of purity with puruṣa; the purity of puruṣa is the absence of figurative (upacarita) experience. In this state kaivalya occurs, whether for the one who has lordship (īśvara) or not, whether he has shared in discrimination-born knowledge or not; for one whose seeds of affliction are burnt no further need of knowledge remains. The power and knowledge born of samādhi were begun by way of the purity of sattva. In ultimate truth it is by knowledge that non-seeing (adarśana) is removed; with that removed, no further afflictions; with no afflictions, no ripening of karma; and in this state the guṇas, their office finished, no longer present themselves to puruṣa as something seen. That is puruṣa's kaivalya: then puruṣa is a light of its own form alone, stainless, isolated (kevalī).
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: Chapter 4 (Kaivalya-pāda, 34 sūtras). (1) 4.1-4.6: the five sources of powers (birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, samādhi); transformation into another birth by the filling in of prakṛti, with dharma and the like as occasion, not impeller; constructed minds from I-ness alone, impelled by one mind, the meditation-born one without residue. (2) 4.7-4.11: the four kinds of karma; the manifestation of vāsanās fitted to the ripening of karma; continuity of vāsanās across birth, place and time because memory and saṃskāra have one form; their beginninglessness; what holds them together (cause, fruit, support, object) and their cessation in its absence. (3) 4.12-4.14: the past and future exist in their own form; the properties are manifest or subtle and of the nature of the guṇas; the reality of a thing from the oneness of transformation. (4) 4.15-4.23: the object and the mind: the object is the same while minds differ and is independent of a single mind; it is known or unknown by the mind's colouring; the mind's modifications are always known to unchanging puruṣa; the mind is not self-luminous because it is seen; regress and confusion of memory if a mind were seen by another; consciousness, not passing over, takes the form of the intellect's modification; the mind coloured by seer and seen is all-objective. (5) 4.24-4.28: the mind, though variegated by countless vāsanās, is for another; cessation of the cultivation of self-becoming for one who sees the distinction; the mind sloping towards kaivalya; other cognitions in its gaps from saṃskāras and their abandoning. (6) 4.29-4.34: dharma-megha samādhi; cessation of afflictions and karma; endless knowledge and the little knowable; the end of the sequence of the guṇas' transformations; sequence and its end; and kaivalya as the return to source of the guṇas empty of puruṣa's purpose, or the establishment of the power of consciousness in its own form.
speaker: Patañjali

paraphrase: Others hold that the mind, like a lamp in a jar or a palace, contracts and expands and is only of the size of the body, so that an intermediate state (antarābhāva) and saṃsāra are logical. The teacher (ācārya) says that it is the function (vṛtti) of the all-pervading (vibhu) mind that contracts and expands, and this depends on dharma and the like as occasion. Occasion is twofold, external and internal: external depends on means such as the body (praise, gift, salutation), internal depends on the mind alone (faith and the like). As was said, the 'abodes' of meditators (friendliness and the rest) bring about exalted dharma without help from external means; of the two the mental is stronger: what surpasses knowledge and dispassion, and who else could empty the Daṇḍaka forest by bodily action without the strength of mind, or drink the ocean like Agastya?
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Two positions on the size of the mind are stated: that of 'others' (the mind takes the size of the body) and that of the ācārya (the mind is all-pervading, only its function contracts and expands). Recorded as the bhāṣya states them; the ontology's dispute entry holds both.

yad abhimukhībhūtaṃ vastu yāṃ vāsanāṃ vyanakti tasyās tadālambanam /

paraphrase: The cause (hetu): from dharma, pleasure; from adharma, pain; from pleasure, attachment; from pain, aversion; from these, effort, by which, moving by mind, speech or body, one favours or harms another; from that again dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion. Thus this six-spoked wheel of saṃsāra turns; ignorance (avidyā) is its leader and the root of all the afflictions. The fruit is that on which the presentness of dharma and the rest depends. The support (āśraya) is the mind with its office still to be done: when the mind's office is finished, the vāsanās, having no support, cannot remain. The object (ālambana) is whatever thing coming to the fore manifests a vāsanā. All vāsanās are held together by these four, and when they are absent the vāsanās depending on them are absent.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: The future is that whose manifestation is to come; the past that whose manifestation has been experienced; the present that which has risen to its own function; these three are objects of knowledge. If they did not exist in their own form, this cognition would arise without an object; therefore the past and future exist in their own form. Also, if the fruit of karma about to arise were unreal (nirupākhya), skilful action aimed at it would not be fitting. The cause is able to make an existing fruit present, not to produce it anew; it only gives a special favour to what depends on it. The bearer (dharmin) has many properties, established in the different paths. The past and future are not present in the manner of the present, with a special manifestation; they exist by the own-form that is to be manifested, or by the own-form of manifestation once experienced. The own-form-manifestation belongs to the present path only. At any time two paths are always attended by the bearer, so the three paths do not come into being from non-existence.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: One common object is the support of many minds; it is not imagined by one mind nor by many minds but stands on itself (sva-pratiṣṭha). How: with the object the same, the cognition differs by the mind: one relying on dharma has cognition of pleasure, one relying on adharma has cognition of pain, one relying on ignorance has deluded cognition, one relying on right seeing has cognition of indifference. An object imagined by one mind cannot colour another's mind. So the path of the object and the path of the cognition, distinguished as grasped and grasping, are separate, with no trace of mixing. On the Sāṃkhya side the object is of three guṇas and moving, connected with minds according to dharma and the like as occasion, and is the cause of the cognition that arises in the form fitting that occasion. Some say the object arises together with cognition because it is enjoyable like pleasure; by this line, obstructing commonness, they deny the form of the object in the earlier and later moments.
speaker: Vyāsa

notes: Vyāsa's account of the view he rejects ('some say') is included as he reports it.

paraphrase: As the other senses and their objects, being seen, are not self-luminous, so the mind is to be understood. If the mind were self-luminous it would be ungraspable by anyone, as ākāśa is established in itself and not in another. But the activity of beings is seen from the awareness of the course of their own intellect ('I am angry, I am afraid, here is my attachment, there my anger'), which would not be fitting if one's own intellect were not grasped.

tathā skandhānāṃ mahannirvedāya virāgāyānutpādāya praśāntaye guror antike brahmacaryaṃ cariṣyāmīty uktvā sattvasya punaḥ sattvam evāpahnuvate /

paraphrase: If a mind were grasped by another mind, by what would the cognition of cognition (buddhi-buddhi) be grasped, and that by another, and that by another: a regress. And memory would be confused: as many memories as there are experiences of these cognitions, and from the confusion there would be no ascertainment of one memory. Thus by the annihilationists (vaināśika), who deny the puruṣa who is aware of the intellect, everything is thrown into confusion; they, imagining an experiencer anywhere, do not cohere by reason. Some, imagining even a 'being' (sattva) who lays down these five aggregates and takes up others, still fear it; and having said 'I shall live the celibate life at the teacher's feet for great disgust with the aggregates, dispassion, non-arising and tranquillity', they then deny the being. The Sāṃkhya-Yoga and other doctrines, by their own word, accept puruṣa as the lord of the mind and the experiencer.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Vyāsa criticises a position he ascribes to the 'vaināśikas'; the criticism is recorded as his, not as a report by the opponents themselves.

paraphrase: The mind is coloured by the object to be thought, and, itself being an object, is connected by its own function with puruṣa the subject. This one mind, coloured by seer and seen, shining as both object and subject, having taken on the form of the conscious and the unconscious, object-natured yet as if not, unconscious yet as if conscious, like a crystal jewel, is called 'all-objective'. Deluded by this likeness of the mind, some say the mind itself is the conscious; others say all this is mind only and there is no world of cows and pots with causes; they are to be pitied, because they have as their seed of delusion the mind shining with the forms of all things. In the insight of samādhi the known object, reflected, is other than the mind, since it is its support; if that object were mind alone, how could the insight determine its own form by insight itself? Therefore the puruṣa by whom the reflected object in the insight is determined exists. Those who distinguish, by class, grasper, grasping and grasped as three differing forms of the mind are right-seers, and by them puruṣa is reached.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Two views are reported by Vyāsa and answered ('some say the mind is the conscious'; 'others say mind only'); no school is named.

paraphrase: This mind, though variegated by countless vāsanās, is for another, for that other's experience and release, not for itself, because it acts in combination, like a house. A mind that acts in combination cannot be for its own sake: the mind of pleasure is not for pleasure, knowledge is not for knowledge; both are for another. The puruṣa who is meaningful by experience and release is the other; not the other as mere generality. Whatever mere-generality 'other' an annihilationist might offer would itself, acting in combination, be only for another. But this special other is puruṣa, who does not act in combination.

paraphrase: The immovable eternity is puruṣa's, the transforming eternity that of the guṇas: that in which, while it transforms, the reality (tattva) is not destroyed is eternal, and both are eternal because their reality is not struck. In the properties of the guṇas such as the intellect, sequence is grasped by the end of transformation and has a final limit; in the guṇas as eternal bearers it has no final limit. For liberated puruṣas, eternal and immovable, established in mere own-form, the being in own-form is experienced only as sequence, imagined by following the word for existence, and there too has no final limit. The bhāṣya then treats the question whether saṃsāra, abiding and moving in the guṇas, has an end of sequence. It sorts questions: 'will everyone born die?' is answered categorically ('yes'); 'will everyone who dies be born?' is answered by distinction (the skilled one whose discrimination-vision has arisen and whose thirst is exhausted will not be born, the other will); 'is human birth better?' is answered by distinction (better than animals, not better than gods and seers). The question 'is this saṃsāra finite or endless?' is called one not answerable as posed (avacanīya); for the skilled one there is an end of the sequence of saṃsāra, not for the other, and fixing on either alone is a fault. Therefore this question is to be answered by analysis (vyākaraṇīya).
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: The passage names 'avacanīya' for the finite-or-endless question and then concludes 'vyākaraṇīya'; both words are recorded as they stand and no further reading is added.

paraphrase: Thesis of the Yoga Sūtra (with Vyāsa's bhāṣya), decided by the six marks of purport. The text teaches yoga, defined as the restraint (nirodha) of the modifications of the mind (1.2), whose result is the seer's abiding in its own form (1.3); the eight limbs (2.29) and saṃyama (3.4) are its means, discriminative vision (2.26, 3.49, 4.29) its ripening, and kaivalya (2.25, 3.50, 3.55, 4.34) its end. (1) Opening and closing (upakrama-upasaṃhāra): the text opens 'now the teaching of yoga' (1.1), defines yoga and states the seer's abiding in its own form (1.2-1.3); it closes with kaivalya as the establishment in its own form of the power of consciousness (4.34), the same abiding in its own form (svarūpa-pratiṣṭhā) as 1.3 names. (2) Repetition (abhyāsa): kaivalya is stated at 2.25, 3.50, 3.55, 4.26, 4.34; the destruction of afflictions as burnt seeds at 2.10, 3.50, 4.28; discriminative vision at 2.26, 3.49, 3.55, 4.29; the distinction between seer and seen or mind and puruṣa at 2.17-2.23, 3.35, 4.18-4.24; saṃskāra and vāsanā at 1.18, 1.50, 3.9-3.10, 4.8-4.11, 4.27-4.28. (3) Novelty (apūrvatā): no verse marks anything as novel or as knowable by no other means; the only self-designation of this kind is the bhāṣya on 3.4 calling 'saṃyama' the treatise's technical term (paribhāṣā). (4) Stated result (phala): the seer's abiding in its own form (1.3), the light of knowledge up to discriminative vision from the limbs (2.28), results attached to each restraint and observance (2.35-2.45), the results of saṃyama (3.5 and 3.16-3.49), cessation of afflictions and karma and the end of the guṇas' sequence (4.30-4.32), kaivalya (4.34). (5) Praise (arthavāda): no verse is a passage of praise as such; the long list of powers (3.16-3.49) is stated as results, and the text itself places them below kaivalya: obstacles in samādhi (3.37), to be met with dispassion (3.50) and without attachment or pride (3.51). Whether any passage functions as praise is left to the interpretation layer (P7). (6) Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): the account of ignorance as the cause of the conjunction of seer and seen (2.15-2.25); the transformations of the mind and elements (3.9-3.15); the argument for the existence of past and future (4.12), for an object independent of any one mind (4.14-4.16), for the mind's being seen and not self-luminous (4.19-4.21), and for puruṣa from the mind's acting in combination for another (4.24).
speaker: Patañjali
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Decided from the sūtras of all four pādas (pādas 1-2 read in the segments for this entry) and Vyāsa's bhāṣya; the reading of the six marks is the extractor's, using only verse references in the text.
